summary:
Three Silences is an interactive website that tells the stories of the machines humanity left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Children spin a 3D Moon or Mars, tap a glowing “ghost rover” and land beside it. The machine then tells its own story in simple words, next to facts checked against NASA records. A time slider replays every landing since 1966, a signal-delay experiment shows why Mars rovers can’t be driven live, and a 3D hangar lets children explore 22 spacecraft part by part. A short graphic novel told by a sleeping Mars lander, and a podcast that opens with the Voyager Golden Record, tell the same history in other ways.

The challenge asks for story-driven learning about abandoned hardware. Children usually hear only about active missions, so the silent ones are forgotten. Three Silences gives them a voice, so that young explorers aged 8–12 feel a personal connection to these machines and understand the science they made possible.
details:
Three Silences — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 submission

Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars Audience: school-age space fans, written for ages 8–12 Format: an interactive website that runs in any modern browser, with no install or sign-in

Fill in before submitting: team name, team members, the public project link and the demo video link. Check the AI-use section below against the current Space Apps rules.

High-level project summary (short field)

Three Silences tells the stories of machines humanity left behind: on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. You spin a 3D Moon or Mars, tap a glowing "ghost rover" and fly down to land beside it. The machine then tells its own story in simple words, backed by facts checked against NASA sources. A digital graphic novel is told by a Mars lander falling asleep in a dust storm. A five-episode podcast follows an instrument's last days, starting with the Voyager Golden Record. A 3D hangar lets children turn 22 spacecraft, light up their parts and answer quiz questions. The goal is for young people to feel a personal connection to these silent explorers and to understand the science each one made possible.

Detailed project description

What it does

The project has four connected parts:

  1. Ghost Rovers: an interactive 3D Moon and Mars map
    • Machines at 18 landing sites, 17 real and one fictional, appear as glowing dots. They include Apollo 11's Eagle, the Apollo 15–17 Moon buggies, Surveyor 3, Lunokhod 1 and 2, Yutu, Yutu-2, Pragyan, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder & Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance and InSight.
    • Tapping a dot makes the camera dive to that spot and land beside a 3D model of the machine. A story card then opens: the machine speaking in its own voice, key numbers, "from the records" facts and a NASA source link.
    • Time slider (1966 → today): shows when each machine arrived and went silent. Rover routes are drawn on the surface. Small text-free arrows point to new landings off-screen.
    • Signal delay: "send a command" and watch the light-speed delay to the Moon (~1.3 s) and to Mars (3–22 min). The page explains why the delay happens.
    • Drive a rover: live, delayed or planned driving, with the keyboard or on-screen buttons. It shows why Mars rovers must be driven with planned command lists.
    • Landing leftovers: the 3D view shows the heat shields, parachutes, backshells and sky cranes left behind at landing sites. Examples are Curiosity's sky crane crash site about 650 m from the rover, and Perseverance's backshell, which Ingenuity photographed in April 2022.
    • Guided tour "Last Signals": a narrated tour with subtitles.
    • It holds 22 spacecraft across the Moon, Mars and deep space, including Mariner 4, Voyager 1 and 2, Pioneer 10, Kepler, Dawn and NEAR Shoemaker. 15 of them are shown with real 3D models from NASA and open libraries.
    • Children can light up parts such as RTGs, the Golden Record or reaction wheels.
    • A dust slider shows how dust reduces solar power.
    • Each spacecraft has a "Cosmic Detective" quiz question.

How it works

  • It is a single HTML page using JavaScript and three.js (WebGL).
  • The Moon and Mars globes, terrain and all spacecraft models are generated in code, so the project needs no large downloads.
  • Narration uses the browser's built-in speech; the piano sounds use the Web Audio API.
  • The signal delay is calculated from the speed of light and an orbital approximation of the Earth–Mars distance.

Accessibility

  • Everything works with a keyboard: Tab and Enter to choose, the arrow keys or W A S D to drive, and Esc to stop.
  • The guided tour has on-screen subtitles and the podcast has a full transcript.
  • 3D views and comic pages have text descriptions for screen readers. Spacecraft that are not NASA's are labelled with their country.
  • Motion is reduced when the device asks for it: no auto-spin and no fly-in animations.
  • The language is simplified for younger readers, and the layout works on phones and tablets.

Benefits and impact

  • Children usually hear only about active missions. This project gives the "retired" machines a voice and shows how their engineering led to discoveries. Examples are airbags that bounced Pathfinder to a safe landing, a broken wheel that helped Spirit find silica, and dust that ended InSight and Opportunity.
  • Interactions such as driving with a delay and blowing dust off panels teach by doing instead of listing facts.
  • Facts and fiction are separated clearly: every machine's voice is fiction, while every "from the records" fact is checked against NASA sources.

Tools used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js r128, Web Audio API and the Web Speech API.

Use of NASA data and resources

Mission facts were checked against these NASA pages:

  • NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 11 Lunar Module, Apollo 12 Lunar Module, Apollo 15 Lunar Module
    • Surveyor 3
    • Viking 1
    • Mars Pathfinder
    • Spirit and Opportunity
    • InSight
    • Ingenuity
    • Pioneer 10
    • Kepler
    • Dawn
    • NEAR Shoemaker
    • Rover's Backshell Seen From the Air (Ingenuity, 2022)
    • Scene of a Martian Landing (HiRISE, Curiosity)

Examples of data used:

  • landing dates and coordinates;
  • distances driven, such as Opportunity's 45.16 km and Perseverance passing it on 11 October 2026;
  • Ingenuity's 72 flights;
  • Pioneer 10's last signal from 12.23 billion km;
  • Kepler's 2,600+ planets;
  • NEAR's 6.4 km/h touchdown on Eros;
  • the distances to landing debris.

Space agency partner resources

Lunokhod 1 and 2 (USSR), Yutu and Yutu-2 (China) and Pragyan (India) are included so the map shows the full picture of the Moon's surface. Each one is labelled as not NASA.

References

  • Team Aether, Astrorelics (NASA Space Apps 2026): mission facts adapted for the 3D Hangar.
  • three.js, MIT License: https://threejs.org
  • All 3D models, textures, the comic art and the podcast audio are generated in code for this project. No copyrighted images or music are used.

Use of artificial intelligence (AI)

  • Coding and text: this project was built with help from an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), which wrote code and drafted the English text.
  • Human review: I selected the story and the design, reviewed the results, and verified the information regarding the task by cross-referencing it with the NASA sources listed above.
  • Generated media: No AI-generated images, videos, or audio files have been used. The visuals and sounds are sourced from the pages linked herein and are generated via code at runtime.

Demo slides link: https://claude.ai/artifact/XsnpCQUBjos2vktVwVtPCG#slide-ecf2dfc2b8e7

Our project demo is a 7-slide presentation (title and introduction included). It walks through the four parts of Three Silences with real screenshots: Ghost Rovers (a 3D Moon and Mars you can land on, with a timeline and a signal-delay experiment), the Sleep Mode graphic novel, The Last Tuning podcast, and the 3D Hangar of 22 spacecraft. It ends with who the project is for and how we kept it accurate. For the full experience, please open the live project link.

Project Details

What it does Three Silences is an interactive website that tells the stories of the machines humanity left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It has four connected parts:

  • Ghost Rovers is a 3D Moon and Mars. You tap a glowing dot and the camera dives down and lands beside the machine, which then tells its own story in simple words, next to facts from NASA records.
    • A time slider replays every landing from 1966 to today.
    • A signal-delay experiment lets you send a command and wait for light to travel: 1.3 seconds to the Moon, up to 22 minutes to Mars.
    • You can drive a rover live, with a delay, or with a plan, and see why Mars rovers can't be steered in real time.
  • Sleep Mode is a short graphic novel told by MIRA-4, a fictional Mars lander, as dust slowly covers its solar panels.
  • The Last Tuning is a five-episode podcast about an instrument's last days. It opens with the Voyager Golden Record, an instrument from Earth that nobody plays.
  • The 3D Hangar holds 22 spacecraft, 15 of them real 3D models. Children can turn them, tap a part to light it up, add dust to solar panels and answer a quiz question on each.

Benefits and intended impact

As for us, I wanted them to get to know the retired machines as well, and to understand the discoveries these machines had made.

My goal is for the children, upon completing the project, to form a personal connection with these silent explorers and to truly grasp scientific concepts—such as signal latency, the accumulation of dust on solar panels, and why landers require rockets in addition to parachutes.

How we built it, and who did what

  • My part:
    • I researched the missions and collected and checked the facts against NASA Science mission pages and the NASA NSSDCA catalogue.
    • I found and prepared the 3D models, from NASA 3D Resources and open 3D libraries.
    • I decided the story, the audience and the look, tested every part, and asked for revisions wherever something was wrong, unclear or not accurate enough.
  • AI assistance: The software was written with the help of an AI assistant, Claude by Anthropic. It wrote the code from my direction, converted and shrank the 3D models, drafted the English text, and I reviewed and corrected the results.
  • Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and three.js (WebGL). Real 3D models came in many formats (GLB, OBJ, FBX, STL and USDZ, some Draco-compressed). We converted them in the browser with three.js loaders, TinyUSDZ and meshoptimizer, so they load quickly. The Moon and Mars globes are generated in code. The piano uses the Web Audio API and the narration uses the Web Speech API. Mission facts for the hangar were adapted from Team Aether's Astrorelics project.

How it is creative The machines speak for themselves. The same history is told in three ways (a map you can land on, a comic and a podcast), so a child can find the one that suits them. Ideas are taught by doing:

  • You feel the delay before a Mars rover moves.
  • You watch power drop as dust builds up.
  • You see the "landing leftovers": the heat shields, parachutes and sky cranes left behind at landing sites.

Factors we considered

  • Age: The language is written for 8–12 year olds.
  • Accuracy: Every "From the records" fact comes from NASA sources. Every machine's voice is fiction and labelled as such. Machines that are not NASA's are marked with their country. On the Moon we show only Eagle's descent stage, because the top half flew away in 1969.
  • Accessibility: It has keyboard controls, subtitles, a full podcast transcript and reduced motion.
  • Performance: It works on phones, and each 3D model loads only when it is opened.
